Description: Science goal and objectives: our goal is to determine the relation between GPS radio signal scintillation and plasma conditions in three key regions in the highlatitude ionosphere (cusp, nightside auroral oval, and polar cap). the goal will be achieved BY addressing three science questions: (1) how are scintillation occurrence and strength related to ionosphere conditions? (2) what types of auroral and airglow forms are related to scintillation? (3) what are the wavenumber spectra of f-region ionosphere density irregularities during scintillation? methodology: the scintillation will be identified using the canadian high arctic ionospheric network (chain) GPS receiver data. the ionosphere density will be obtained from tec given BY individual receiver-satellite combinations. the flow velocity will be obtained from the superdarn radars and swarm satellites. THEMIS and rego all-sky imagers will be used to determine auroral intensity and structure. the density irregularity spectra will be provided from the swarm satellites. CASE studies and linear correlation analyses will be performed for determining the relation among scintillation, tec, flow velocity, auroral intensity, and their gradients. nonlinear correlations and causality will be identified through the application of information theory. for nightside and polar cap scintillation, the imager data will be used to find the types of auroral and airglow forms for identifying what auroral forms and airglow structures are related to scintillation occurrence. when the swarm satellites are in conjunction with the chain network, the slope of the density wavenumber spectra will be calculated to find what cascading processes contribute to formation of density irregularities. the findings from these works will be used to identify what type of instability (e.g, gradient drift instability and kelvin-helmholtz instability) is consistent with the observation. proposed contributions to the fst effort and relevance to the fst: the proposed study will provide observational specification of the occurrence conditions of the scintillation in the high-latitude ionosphere. the relation between scintillation and ionospheric structures (tec, flow, precipitation and in-situ density structure) will observationally show what types of forcing to the ionosphere are important for creating scintillation, and what instability mechanisms explain the scintillation occurrence. these expected findings will directly address the goal of the fst "understand and model the conditions that lead to the onset and evolution of ionospheric irregularities and resulting scintillation events at low, mid and high latitudes.", and two of the fst objectives "identify the mechanisms and structures that are responsible for ionospheric irregularities and scintillations " and "identify the instability mechanisms responsible for polar f-region irregularities". the observational work is complementary to proposals that will conduct numerical simulations of scintillation. our work will provide observational constraints of the simulation setup of ionosphere conditions and will assist interpretation of the physical mechanisms of simulated density irregularities and scintillation. information theory CAN also provide a novel approach to model verifications and validations. the traditional model-data comparison methodology of comparing simulation with data at a particular point in space and time CAN be supplemented with comparing information flow from input to intermediate and to output variables in the simulation and observational data. our work on high-latitude scintillation in north america is complementary to studies of scintillation at low/midlatitudes and other longitudes/hemispheres and will contribute for comparing similarities and differences in scintillation at various regions.

Description: Spacecraft (S/C) crossing the magnetopause often observe a single transient structure or a series of bipolar signatures in the magnetic field component normal to the magnetopause (bn). numerous observations of these signatures, termed AS flux transfer events (ftes), have established their typical signatures, including enhanced magnetic field strength due to a strong core field at/around the bn reversal. most of these signatures have been explained BY their generation via single- or multiple-x-line reconnection. however, a large portion of observed ftes displays more complex core field signatures than a simple enhancement. the core field maximum CAN be bracketed BY two minima, or the core field enhancement CAN display a local minimum NEAR the center. these types of ftes are commonly referred to AS crater ftes and the two distinct profiles have been described AS w- and m-shaped. although these crater ftes have been proposed to be early-stage ftes, or associated with a back-and-forth S/C motion relative to typical ftes or a separatrix crossing, the substructures and formation mechanism of atypical ftes including crater ftes have not been established. furthermore, recent observations indicate that magnetic reconnection occurring at the leading edge or at the center of ftes may erode magnetic flux contained in ftes, thus contributing to the evolution of ftes and their structures. the goal of this project is to discover the kinetic processes underlying various substructures of atypical ftes and to understand how these micro (electron)-to-meso (ion)-scale dynamics determine the meso-to-macroscopic properties and time-varying nature of ftes. this goal is achieved BY completing two objectives: o1: determine the kinetic processes underlying atypical ftes with different substructures. o2: understand how kinetic processes determine cross-scale properties and evolution of ftes. BY completing these two objectives, we determine how localized dynamics such AS reconnection, flow shear, wave activity, and energy dissipation regulate the characteristics of ftes, constructing the full context of topology and evolution of  typical atypical ftes . to complete o1-2, to complete these objectives, we utilize a combination of observational and theoretical methodologies. this combination incorporates the ample MMS observations of atypical ftes, reconstruction techniques, particle-in-cell (pic) simulations, and theoretical analysis. MMS with its high-resolution measurements enables us to resolve the detailed substructures of ftes. fours/ c analyses, including force analysis and quantitative testing of kinetic-scale physics, allow us to investigate the micro/meso-scale physics underlying substructures of ftes (o1). we additionally use ACE/wind/geotail/cluster/THEMIS/artemis/DSCOVR data to determine SOLAR wind and boundary conditions for fte occurrences. we employ 4-S/C observations of ftes to place their spatio-temporal variations in context of cross-scale properties and evolution of ftes (o2). BY synthesizing in-situ observations and simulations, we determine whether or not the local kinetic dynamics link to certain types of atypical ftes and how these physical processes lead to energy conversion and regulate the evolution of ftes, which are highly relevant to the coupling of the SOLAR wind and earth s magnetosphere. understanding the formation, structure, and evolution of ftes improves our understanding of the connections between SOLAR variability and earth space environments, directly relevant to the heliophysics overarching goal. in particular, our program addresses one of the most fundamental physical processes, i.e., magnetic reconnection that occurs from the sun to the heliosphere and throughout the universe, which is entirely relevant to the goals of the MMS mission.
